title: What happens after independence?
essentialQuestion: Why does making schools work for every child take longer than one day of independence?
learningGoal: Explain why rebuilding education in Timor-Leste took years, using two sources, and say what a photo of a school cannot show.

warmUp.question: A school needs a building. What else does it need so children can learn?
options: Lessons in a language children know

evidence.question: Which source tells you when something happened? Which tells you how schools were rebuilt? Which shows one school today?

cards.title: Real sources about schools in Timor-Leste

sources.caption: Source 1: The United Nations' background page on East Timor, written for its peacekeeping missions
details: It says East Timorese voters took part in a UN-organised vote on 30 August 1999, and most chose to begin a move towards independence.
It says a UN transitional administration ran the territory from October 1999, working more and more with East Timorese leaders.
It says Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002.
Limit: it records dates and decisions, not what happened inside schools.

sources.caption: Source 2: A United Nations news report from March 2000, during the transition
details: It says most children who had been in primary school in 1998 and 1999 were back in class.
It says many schools had been repaired, and roofing materials had been given to schools.
It says there was no standard curriculum yet, and classes were taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English.
Limit: it is a short report on numbers. It does not tell us what lessons were like for one child.

sources.caption: Source 3: "Learning independence", a study by Susan Nicolai for UNESCO's education planning institute (IIEP), 2004
details: It looks back at how schooling restarted after 1999.
It says rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans and rules for education.
It also looks at language, teachers' training and classroom materials.
Limit: it is a study written later, not a diary from a school in 1999.

sources.caption: Source 4: A photo of a school in Timor-Leste, taken on 21 November 2024 by Ponsyano
details: It shows one school building with a red roof and ramps.
Limit: it shows one place in 2024. It cannot show whether students have books, trained teachers or lessons they understand.

cards.title: A milestone inside a longer story

events.text: East Timorese voters take part in a UN-organised vote.
The UN reports that most primary school children are back in class.
Susan Nicolai's study for UNESCO looks back at education since 1999.
Ponsyano photographs a school in Timor-Leste.

sections.heading: A vote, a transition and restored independence
sections.text: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote run by the United Nations. Most voted to begin a move towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. A transition followed. A United Nations team ran the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. It had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate on one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.
sections.simpler: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition. A United Nations team helped run the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate in one day. But good schools for every child take much longer.

sections.heading: A researcher's evidence
sections.text: Rebuilding schools began during the transition, not after it. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children who had been in primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped restart their schools. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher called Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events. It is not a diary written by a child in 1999.
sections.simpler: Work on schools started during the transition. It did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report said most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people fixed buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.

sections.heading: Choices after 2002
sections.text: The Government of Timor-Leste lists Tetum and Portuguese as the official languages. People also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the United Nations' agency for children, says the country has rebuilt its schools since 2002, and more children now go to school. It also names problems: old buildings, many languages, and fewer school facilities in country areas. UNICEF works with the government on school repairs, teaching and schools where students and parents take part. The photo shows one school in 2024. It cannot tell us if students there have books or trained teachers. It cannot show if they have access to lessons in a language they know.
sections.simpler: Timor-Leste has two official languages. They are Tetum and Portuguese. People speak many other languages too. UNICEF works for children. It says more children go to school now. But there are still problems. Some buildings are old. Some places far from towns have fewer schools. The photo shows one school in 2024. It does not show if students have books. It does not show if they have access to lessons they understand.

glossary.definition: A time of change from one way of running things to another.
glossary.example: During the transition, a United Nations team helped run East Timor.

glossary.definition: Given back, or made to work again.
glossary.example: Timor-Leste's independence was restored on 20 May 2002.

glossary.definition: The plan for what students learn in school.
glossary.example: In 2000, there was no standard curriculum for East Timor's schools.

glossary.definition: A language a government uses for laws and public work.
glossary.example: Tetum and Portuguese are Timor-Leste's official languages.

glossary.definition: A real chance to go somewhere and use it, not only a building nearby.
glossary.example: Access to school means a child can get there and learn.

checks.question: When did work to rebuild schools in Timor-Leste begin?

options.feedback: Not quite. Schools were already being repaired in 2000. Look at the start of the second part of the reading.
Not quite. That is much too late. Look for the UN report in the second part of the reading.
Yes. A UN report in 2000 said many schools were repaired. The work went on after 2002.

checks.question: The school photo was taken in 2024. What can it show?

options.feedback: Not quite. A photo of a building cannot show what teachers know. Look at the end of the reading.
Yes. It shows one building on one day. It cannot show what every student lives through.
Not quite. One photo cannot show every student's learning. You would need to ask students and teachers.

checks.placeholder: For example: A student would also need ... because ...

write.prompt: Choose two things to work on first in a new school system. Give a reason from the sources for each. Then name one trade-off or question.
sentenceStarters: I would ask students and teachers ...
selfCheck: I chose two things to work on first.
I gave a reason from the sources for each.
I named one trade-off or question.
write.example: My first choice is safe classrooms. The UN report says many schools needed repairs after 1999. My second choice is books in languages students understand. Teachers used four languages, and there was no curriculum yet. The sources show that buildings alone are not enough. One trade-off is that money spent on buildings cannot also train teachers. I would ask students and teachers what they need first.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, decide which two groups of people should help plan schools. Say one question you would ask each group.
speak.independentTask: Record a short voice note or write a short paragraph: name two groups who should help plan schools, and one question for each.

watch.title: In Timor-Leste, UNICEF joins government child-friendly efforts to rebuild education
watch.why: This short UNICEF report from 2011 visits one school and shows how teachers, parents and the government worked to restart education after 1999.
watch.beforeQuestion: What would a school need to start again after a hard time?
watch.afterQuestion: Who helped the school in Laclubar start again after 1999?
watch.summary: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. It visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountains of Timor-Leste. After the vote in 1999, many people left their homes. The school was left with no roof, desks or chairs. When people came back, local school leaders asked teachers to return. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education says the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, fix schools and train teachers. Now the school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Students and parents take part in school life.
keyPoints: After 1999, many schools had to start again from the beginning.
Local school leaders, teachers and parents worked together to restart one school.
The government and UNICEF worked to plan new lessons, fix schools and train teachers.
watch.contentNote: Not yet watched by a person. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 1 November 2026; length (3:14) and date (16 May 2011) from YouTube. The summary is written from the video's description and from the text of UNICEF's companion web story by Steve Nettleton (13 May 2011), which unicef.org no longer hosts; I read it in a copy on a Timorese blog. It is not based on the video's words. Preview it: the companion story describes the violence after the 1999 vote (burning and killing) and says many school buildings were burned, so the video may describe this or show damaged buildings. It is a 2011 report, not footage from 1999–2002. Check for advertising before the video.

visual.description: An original Thinkerwell timeline in three stages, left to right, joined by plain arrows: "1999: vote, then transition" → "20 May 2002: independence restored" → "continuing education work" (an open-ended arrow running off the right edge, showing the work goes on). Under the first stage, a small note: "schools restarting", so it is clear education work began before 2002. Around the third stage, four small rounded decision bubbles, each with a simple icon: "buildings" (a roof), "teachers" (a simple figure at a board, no face), "languages and materials" (a book), "access" (a path to a door). No before-and-after score, no progress bar, no flags, no damaged buildings, soldiers or people in distress.
visual.alt: A timeline in three stages: the 1999 vote and transition, with schools restarting; independence restored on 20 May 2002; and education work that continues. Around the last stage are four bubbles: buildings, teachers, languages and materials, and access.
visual.caption: A Thinkerwell timeline of schools in Timor-Leste. It shows that the work began before 2002, and that it goes on today.
visual.lookClosely: Which tasks take longer than a single day?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "School Timor.jpg" by Ponsyano, taken 21 November 2024, described on the file page as "School of Timor-Leste, Eskola SD": a single-storey school building with a red roof, yellow and grey walls and a covered walkway with ramps, on a grassy field, with hills and another red-roofed building behind. Chosen because it is a clearly dated, CC0 photo of a real school in Timor-Leste, which lets learners practise saying what a photo of a building can and cannot show about learning. The colours look digitally boosted.

sensitiveNotes: The 1999 vote was followed by serious violence and the displacement of many people. The lesson says so in one plain sentence; do not add detail or images. Some learners have lived through violence or had to leave their homes: never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, violence or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and let anyone step out of a discussion without a reason. Timor-Leste's history with Indonesia may be sensitive for learners and staff in Indonesia: keep to the dated facts in the lesson, without blame or argument. Preview the video first: its companion story mentions burning and killing in 1999.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners choose two priorities for rebuilding education, give a source-based reason for each, and name a trade-off. Evidence move: ask what a school needs besides walls. A sound answer gives two priorities supported by the UN report, the IIEP study or UNICEF, and a reasonable trade-off. Misconceptions to address: "independence instantly solved education", "education work only started after 2002", and "all learners speak both official languages".

Languages: the Government of Timor-Leste lists Portuguese and Tetum (Tétum, the national language) as official, English and Indonesian as working languages, and about 15 other local languages. Talk about this without deficit framing: many languages are a strength and a planning question, not a problem in children. Source caveats: UNICEF's page gives percentages with no date, so the lesson does not use them as current rates. The IIEP abstract dates the consultation to September 1999 (the vote was on 30 August; the result came in September). The UN news item shows only "23 March"; its address and content (UNTAET, the earlier international force) place it in 2000.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.

Checked against the pages I opened: UNMISET background (30 August 1999 consultation; UNTAET set up on 25 October 1999; 20 May 2002), Government of Timor-Leste (official languages Portuguese and Tétum; independence declared 28 November 1975, restored 20 May 2002), the IIEP abstract (Nicolai, 2004: reconstruction emphasised physical infrastructure over policy; language policy, teacher qualifications and classroom resources) and UNICEF's quality education page (rebuilt education system since 2002; ageing facilities, language diversity, fewer facilities in rural areas; child-friendly schools, student councils, parents).

Added a UN news report from March 2000 (found while checking): most children who had been in primary school back in class, schools repaired, roofing materials given, no standard curriculum, teaching in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. It gives a dated, official source for the brief's point that rebuilding began during the transition.

Added one line on why independence was "restored" (first declared in 1975, from the government page) and one plain sentence that violence and displacement followed the 1999 vote, with no detail. Left out UNICEF's undated percentages.
Used "Tetum" in learner text (the UN's spelling); the government page writes "Tétum". A reviewer may prefer one spelling for the course.

Commons file checked through the Commons API on 1 November 2026: Ponsyano, own work, 21 November 2024, CC0, as the brief says; its description reads "School of Timor-Leste, Eskola SD". Alt text written from the image.

Watch: kept the brief's candidate, UNICEF's "In Timor-Leste, UNICEF joins government child-friendly efforts to rebuild education" (2011, 3:14), because it is short, from UNICEF and about restarting one school. Its summary comes from the description and UNICEF's companion story, not the video. Someone on the team must watch it before learners see it, especially for how it shows 1999.
